sections.h2: What is it like to sell a house in Lawrence Township, NJ?
sections.html:
Lawrence Township is a Mercer County suburb between Trenton and Princeton, and a sale here is shaped by a township housing inspection that has its own application, fee and waiting period. Plan for that step early, because it can take longer than the rest of the closing paperwork.

The township covers 21.73 square miles of land, with 34,165 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, up from 33,077 in the 2020 count. Many people say Lawrenceville when they mean the whole township, since most addresses carry a Lawrenceville mailing label, while others have Princeton or Trenton mailing addresses. Write the legal municipality on any contract so the township, not the postal name, controls which rules apply.

sections.h2: How did Lawrence Township get its name and layout?
sections.html:
The area was set up as Maidenhead Township on February 20, 1697, named by Quaker settlers for a village on the Thames. It was renamed Lawrence Township on January 24, 1816, after a naval captain from the War of 1812, and it joined Mercer County when that county was created on February 22, 1838.

Today the township has a historic village center in Lawrenceville (3,751 residents in 2020) and many named neighborhoods around it, including Slackwood, Eldridge Park, Colonial Lakelands, Port Mercer, Lawrence Station and Quaker Bridge. Stony Brook drains the north toward Princeton and Shabakunk Creek runs south toward Trenton. A tornado in September 2003 followed Princeton Pike and damaged homes, which is worth remembering when a buyer asks about roof age.

sections.h2: What do the Lawrence housing numbers show?
sections.html:
Two thirds of homes here are lived in by their owners, and the typical household earns well above the national figure. The Census reports a median owner-occupied value of $439,700 for 2020 to 2024.

Gross rent runs about $2,020 a month against $2,933 in owner costs with a mortgage. The township has no rent control ordinance outside a short list of affordable-housing complexes.

sections.h2: What jobs, schools and shopping affect Lawrence home values?
sections.html:
Lawrence is a work destination, not just a bedroom town. The Educational Testing Service has been headquartered here since 1964, Bristol Myers Squibb runs a research and development division in the township, and Quaker Bridge Mall, opened in 1975 on U.S. 1, holds more than 100 retailers. Rider University, founded in 1865, sits just south of Lawrenceville, and the Lawrenceville School dates from 1810.

Public schools sit in the Lawrence Township Public Schools district, which had seven schools and 3,707 students in 2020-21. Those are Eldridge Park, Ben Franklin, Lawrenceville and Slackwood elementary schools, Lawrence Intermediate School for grades 4 to 6, Lawrence Middle School and Lawrence High School. Notre Dame High School and Saint Ann School are the Catholic options, and Mercer County Technical Schools take applications from eighth graders countywide.

sections.h2: How do commuters reach Lawrence Township?
sections.html:
Buyers check the commute first. Interstate 295 loops through the township and U.S. 1 splits it, while U.S. 206 (Lawrence Road) is the main local artery from Trenton to Princeton. County routes 533, 546 and 569 handle cross-town trips.

  • Rail: Northeast Corridor trains run along the eastern edge, with the nearest stations in Hamilton, Trenton, Princeton and Princeton Junction.
  • Bus: NJ Transit routes 600, 603, 605, 606, 609 and 613 serve Trenton, and route 612 is local.
  • Air: Trenton-Mercer Airport is in neighboring Ewing, and Philadelphia and Newark airports are about equally far.

Highlight the nearest station and highway ramp in your listing or offer conversation.

sections.h2: What is the Certificate of Inspection for a Lawrence Township sale?
sections.html:
Lawrence Township's Housing office issues a Certificate of Inspection for a sale, and the seller is generally responsible for getting it. A Certificate of Occupancy is a different document, issued by the Construction Official for new work or major renovations. The sale certificate must be in hand before ownership transfers, including condos and foreclosures.

  • Cost and filing: an $80 fee with the application, delivered in person or by mail. No emailed forms or electronic payments are taken.
  • Scheduling: the office needs the application and fee before it will book a visit, and it says it usually schedules within two weeks, sometimes longer.
  • Visit length: about 60 to 90 minutes for a single or two-family house and about 30 minutes for a condo or townhouse.
  • Validity: one year from the inspection date. Re-inspection carries no fee.
  • Safety items: smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers are checked during the same visit, so no separate certificate is required.

A buyer may assume most violations by sending the township a letter naming them and a repair date. Life safety violations still have to be fixed and re-inspected before anyone occupies the house, and a failed septic system or outstanding permits must be settled by the seller before closing. For an as-is or bank-owned sale, the buyer may be the one who obtains the certificate, so settle that point in the contract. The township's Pre-Inspection Checklist lists the common items.

sections.h2: How are the deed and transfer costs handled in Mercer County?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded by the Mercer County Clerk at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. The clerk's fee schedule lists $43 for the first page of a regular deed and $10 for each added page. The records room is open to the public from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays.

The seller owes the state realty transfer fee. With a $439,700 median value, many Lawrence sales fall in the over-$350,000 schedule, which runs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. For deeds over $1 million recorded since July 10, 2025, the county clerk notes a revised fee under a new state law, with the seller responsible.

Mercer County asks that realty transfer fees be paid by cash, cashier's check, money order or an attorney or business escrow account, and amounts over $10,000 by certified or bank check. Your closing attorney or title company normally handles this.

sections.h2: Which way should I sell a Lawrence house?
sections.html:
If the house is in good shape and you can wait for showings, a listing can bring the widest buyer pool in a township with this much commuter demand. If the house needs repairs, has tenants, or the inspection date is a problem, an as-is cash purchase may fit better. Ask each buyer in writing who orders and pays for the Certificate of Inspection and how a failed item will be handled.

Before you decide, call the Housing office at 609-844-7032 to ask for the next open inspection slot. Because the office does not expedite appointments, that date often sets the earliest possible closing.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection to sell a house in Lawrence Township?
faqs.a: Yes. The township requires a Certificate of Inspection before ownership transfers. The seller usually obtains it with an application and an $80 fee, and the certificate expires one year after the visit.

faqs.q: How long does it take to schedule the Lawrence inspection?
faqs.a: About two weeks in most cases, sometimes longer around holidays and busy periods. The office does not expedite appointments and will not book until it has the application and fee.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take over violations from the inspection?
faqs.a: Yes, for most items. The buyer writes the township naming the violations and a correction date. Life safety violations must still be fixed and re-inspected before anyone occupies the house, and the seller must resolve a failed septic system or outstanding permits.

faqs.q: Where is a deed recorded for a Lawrence Township house?
faqs.a: With the Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. The clerk lists deed recording at $43 for the first page plus $10 for each added page.

faqs.q: Does Lawrence Township have rent control?
faqs.a: No, apart from a short list of affordable-housing complexes named by the Housing office. Most single-family rentals and owner-occupied houses are not covered.
